catalog_locator: Section 4.3 'Pronunciation Adaptation', thesis pp. 198-199 (PDF pages 210-211); the stress statement is on thesis p. 199 = PDF page 211. File: the copy we hold…
catalog_quote: In general, pronunciation of utterances, whatever their original sources are, is based on Malay or BI pronunciation. Modification of pronunciation (stress pattern, tone, and phonemes) of Chinese (Hokkien and Mandarin) and Dutch loan words, integrated, and code-switched utterances is a common feature in Peranakan speech. ... Unlike Tagalog, Malay/BI is a language with predictable stress, and the Chinese loan words or integrated utterances get the Malay/BI stress patterns. Primary stress on the first syllable of disyllabic utterances and primary stress on the second syllable of polysyllabic utterances are also valid for Hokkien and Mandarin utterances. The lost of tones in Hokkien loan words can cause ambiguity, although it may be solved by the context of the discourse. The utterence kɔ may mean 'brother' or 'father's sister'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Peranakan speech takes over the 'predictable' Malay/Indonesian stress pattern, which the author states as: primary stress on the first syllable of disyllabic words and on the second syllable of longer words; Chinese loans lose their tones and receive this same pattern. For 2- and 3-syllable words this is the penultimate syllable, which is how the Malay/BI pattern is usually described and how the author frames it; his literal wording ('second syllable of polysyllabic utterances') would place stress on the antepenult in 4-syllable words, so the penult reading is provisional and the literal rule is a peninitial-with-nonfinality one.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the passage is about detonalised Hokkien and Mandarin loans receiving the pattern (ambiguity of homophonous ko 'brother'/'father's sister' after tone loss).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('utterances' = words/loan items) in Peranakan speech of Surabaya, East Java; stated by a sociolinguist in a code-switching thesis, not an instrumental or dedicated phonological study; the stress claim is a one-sentence generalisation transferred from Malay/BI rather than an independent analysis of Peranakan data.
new_statements.identity_note: Kartawinata 1990 describes 'Peranakan speech' of Surabaya, East Java (Malay/Indonesian-based with Javanese, Hokkien, Mandarin and Dutch elements), which is the variety ISO 639-3 'pea' / Glottolog pera1256 denotes (East Java Peranakan Indonesian; Oetomo 1987 covers Pasuruan, Rafferty 1982 and Dreyfuss & Oka 1979 cover Malang). Wolff 1997 concerns the Central Java Peranakan speech, which is a Javanese dialect and not pera1256.

sources.note: Section 3.1 (pp. 55-59) on East Java Indonesian (incl. PCI = Peranakan Chinese Indonesian) phonology gives only indirect hints: lax stops pharyngealised 'in initial position or in stressed syllable' (pp. 55-56); /e/ dropped 'in an unstressed syllable of the antipenult or earlier in the word.. but not in the final syllable' (p. 59). sources.note: Nothing on stress; phonological identity markers limited to glottal-stop insertion and vowel lowering. Describes Central Java Peranakan speech (Javanese-based), not the East Java Indonesian-based variety pera1256.

Only 'sentence stress' is mentioned (p. 80: Javanese/Malay-Indonesian speakers use high pitch on the syllable with sentence stress). No word-stress statement.
